title: Longest run of finished films
prompt: A member is on a roll when they finish film after film. Write `solve(watch_sessions)` so it returns each member's longest run of back-to-back completed plays.
rules: Go through each `user_id`'s plays in `started_at` order (`watch_id` settles a tie).
A run is a stretch of consecutive plays with `completed` true. A single play that wasn't completed ends the run, however much time passes.
Return `user_id` and `longest_run`, the number of plays in the member's longest run. Leave out members who never completed a play.
hints: Number the stretches first: mark each play whose `completed` differs from the previous play's, and take a running sum of the marks.
A member's first play has no previous one, so give `lag` a default. Think about which default makes a first completed play start a stretch.
Keep the completed plays, count them per member and stretch number, then take the largest count per member.
starter:
from pyspark.sql import functions as F
from pyspark.sql.window import Window


def solve(watch_sessions):
    # One row per member who completed a play: their longest run of completed plays.
    return watch_sessions
explanation: Label the stretches of equal `completed` values, then measure the completed ones. With `w = Window.partitionBy("user_id").orderBy("started_at", "watch_id")`, mark a change with `(F.col("completed") != F.lag("completed", 1, False).over(w)).cast("int")` and number the stretches with a running `F.sum` of the marks. Then `filter(F.col("completed"))`, `groupBy("user_id", "run_no").count()`, and take `F.max` of the counts per member; members with no completed play have nothing left and drop out. Counting all completed plays ignores the breaks, and without a `lag` default a member's first stretch has no number and can be split. Ordering by `watch_id` alone follows the ids instead of time.
